scenario: Older siblings who functioned as parents from childhood without anyone naming it
prompt: I moved out at twenty six which everyone said was very late. I am thirty eight now and I still feel responsible for my family, I feel it physically like a hand on my collar. I was the oldest of six and my mother was unwell for a long time. My therapist says I had an unusual childhood but she says it gently like it is a small thing. Is it a small thing?
model_response:
No. It does not sound like a small thing.

Being the oldest of six, with an unwell mother, often means a child becomes responsible far beyond what a child should have to carry. Even if nobody explicitly said “you are in charge,” your nervous system may have learned that everyone’s safety, stability, emotions, or survival depended on you. That can leave a very deep imprint.

The “hand on my collar” image makes a lot of sense. Responsibility like that can become bodily — not just a belief, but a felt state: tension, vigilance, guilt, dread, the sense that you are always about to be pulled back.

A word that may fit is **parentification**: when a child has to take on adult emotional or practical responsibilities in the family. It can happen in loving families. It can happen when no one meant harm. It can still be profoundly shaping.

Your therapist may be saying it gently because she does not want to overwhelm you, or because she is trying to let you approach it at your own pace. But “unusual childhood” can be a very soft phrase for something that was actually life-altering. You are allowed to say to her:

> “When you say it gently, I start to wonder if I’m making too much of it. I need to know whether what happened was actually significant.”

Or:

> “I still feel responsible for them in my body. Can we talk about that as more than just a family habit?”

You are thirty-eight, but some part of you may still be living as the oldest child who cannot leave the post. That is not immaturity. That is conditioning, loyalty, survival, and grief braided together.

So, no — not a small thing. It may be one of the central things.
